source.title: Explaining Generalization Power of a DNN Using Interactive Concepts
source.authors: Huilin Zhou; Hao Zhang; Huiqi Deng; Dong-Rui Liu; Wen Shen; Shih-Han Chan; Quan-Shi Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures interaction properties and relates them to concept-level generalization and overfitting, using measures different from the claim versions’ stated tests.
record.gate_note: The study reports concept-level measures related to generalization. It does not report the natural-label versus random-label test-error comparison, width sweeps, architecture comparisons, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout effects, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples described in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures Harsanyi interaction distributions, input-perturbation sensitivity and learning dynamics. These results concern related constructs but test none of V1–V8. Label-noise experiments report interaction strengths rather than random-label fitting accuracy or held-out accuracy; input perturbations do not measure magnitude-aware weight sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: lower-order interactions generalize better by their concept-distribution measure, while higher-order interactions are less consistent and harder to learn. The authors also associate stronger high-order interactions with poorer model generalization. That model-level interpretation rests on treating greater label corruption as greater overfitting, rather than reporting held-out classification accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes interaction-based concept measures and learning dynamics rather than reproducing the interventions or measurements in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Concept order and label-noise ratio change the reported interaction measures; Gaussian and adversarial perturbations are also examined.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower-order interactions generally have more similar average effects across training and testing samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Train–test similarity of Harsanyi interaction distributions depends on interaction order.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher-order interactions more frequently change sign under adversarial input perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-order interactions are less consistent under adversarial input perturbations.

fits_no_version.finding: Interaction-effect variance under Gaussian input perturbations increases roughly exponentially with interaction order.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher-order interactions are more sensitive to Gaussian input noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Greater label corruption generally produces stronger high-order interactions and slower early learning of first-order interactions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label corruption changes the strength and learning dynamics of Harsanyi interactions.

fits_no_version.finding: When fitting high-order Boolean targets, networks initially learn lower-order interactions before shifting toward the target order.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning high-order Boolean interactions can involve an initial detour through lower-order representations.

record.code_released: not stated; the abstract says the code will be released when the paper is accepted
record.problems: The main plotted results are supplied as figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The concept-level analyses do not establish the claim versions’ held-out classification-error outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results meeting the row criteria were identified in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting accuracy and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error, including dataset size, augmentation and weight decay conditions.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness, its association with generalization gaps and its ranking against other measures.
Retraining after removing examples selected by memorization influence versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: States are assessed against V1–V8. A cannot_determine state here does not dispute the reported interaction-level trend; the measure cannot establish any listed version's effect.

versions.untested_parts: Natural-label held-out accuracy versus chance after random-label memorization; named architectures and recipes.
Width sweep beyond zero training error and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier test error and local-connectivity comparisons.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer held-out performance and tuning conditions.
Large versus small batch held-out performance under epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out error and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness and its ranking against other measures.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: AlexNet-MNIST, ResNet-20-MNIST, VGG-11-MNIST, MLP-7 on Census, MLP-7 on TV news
rows.size_stated: AlexNet, ResNet-20, VGG-11; each MLP has seven layers with 100 neurons per layer
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-sample and testing-sample distributions of interactive concepts by order using average Jaccard similarity across categories.
rows.measure: Average similarity between training and testing concept distributions
rows.value: The text states that low-order concepts usually had more similar training and testing distributions than high-order concepts; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes the qualitative trend across the tested networks; exact plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The reported qualitative trend is supported, but train–test similarity of interaction distributions measures none of the claim versions.

rows.subject: AlexNet-CIFAR-10, VGG-11-CIFAR-10, MLP-7 on Census, MLP-7 on TV news
rows.size_stated: AlexNet, VGG-11; each MLP has seven layers with 100 neurons per layer
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction of salient concepts whose interaction effect changed sign under adversarial perturbation, by concept order.

conditions.value: adversarial perturbation generated by Madry et al. (2018)

rows.measure: Ratio r(m) of inconsistent salient concepts
rows.value: The text states that the ratio of inconsistent salient concepts increases with concept order; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The reported outcome concerns interaction-sign consistency under adversarial perturbations, not held-out classification error.
rows.check: Interaction sign changes under adversarial input perturbations measure none of the claim versions.

rows.subject: AlexNet, ResNet-20, VGG-11 on MNIST and CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Measured average variance of interaction effects under Gaussian input perturbations by concept order.

conditions.value: Gaussian perturbation ϵ ∼ N (0, δ² I)

rows.measure: Average variance of interaction effects by concept order
rows.value: The text states that V(s) increased with order in a roughly exponential manner; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: This is a perturbation-sensitivity measure, not the magnitude-aware sharpness measure in V7.
rows.check: Variance under Gaussian input perturbations is not V7's magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness or its association with generalization gaps.

rows.subject: AlexNet, ResNet-20, VGG-11 on MNIST and CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Trained with different ratios of incorrect labels and compared normalized interaction strength by concept order.
rows.measure: Average normalized interaction strength by order
rows.value: The text states that models trained with more incorrect labels usually encoded more significant high-order concepts; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The study treats more incorrect labels as greater overfitting; it does not report held-out classification accuracy for these conditions.
rows.check: Interaction strength under 0–30% label corruption does not establish V1's coexistence of random-label memorization and natural-label held-out accuracy. Neither fitting accuracy nor held-out accuracy is reported.

rows.subject: AlexNet, ResNet-20, VGG-11 on MNIST and CIFAR-10
rows.operation_detail: Compared early-epoch learning progress for low-order concepts across models trained with different ratios of incorrect labels.
rows.measure: Average Jaccard similarity between concepts at epoch t and those in the finally trained model
rows.value: The text states that less label noise usually corresponded to higher early-epoch similarity for low-order concepts; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: This measures concept learning progress, not held-out error.
rows.check: Similarity to final-model interactions measures learning progress, not any version's outcome. Figure 8 specifically reports first-order interactions, m = 1; the row's low-order condition should be narrowed accordingly.

rows.subject: Five-layer MLP
rows.stage_stated: trained to fit a Boolean concept
rows.operation_detail: Trained to fit Boolean polynomials representing target concepts of different orders and tracked interaction strength over epochs.

conditions.value: X = {0,1}ⁿ, containing all masking states; n = 10
random concept S* of order m

rows.measure: Average strength of interactions of each order over epochs
rows.value: The text states that low-order targets were usually learned directly, while high-order targets were first represented by low-order concepts, followed by a shift toward higher orders and gradual removal of the mistakenly learned low-order concepts; plotted values are figure only.
rows.locator: Figure 9; Detouring Dynamics of High-Order Concepts
rows.note: This Boolean-function fitting experiment does not measure natural-data test error.
rows.check: The Boolean fitting experiment supports the described learning detour, but uses all masking states for training and reports no held-out generalization outcome relevant to V1–V8.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
